activity.title: You don't need to hire an ML team to get smarter e-commerce search. Instead, just wrap your existing search API in an agent and see what happens. We did exactly that – agent in front of a basic keyword search, same API, no UX change. Ran it against a Wayfair-style furniture dataset with 100 labeled queries. The agent did some genuinely clever stuff (sectional = modular sofa, when to quote "dress shoes," broad-then-narrow). It also occasionally did some dumb stuff (hallucinated filter values, over-constrained first queries), which we largely fixed with better prompting and some few-shot examples. Net result: ~6–10% gain in NDCG depending on prompt. Full writeup, diagrams, and the tradeoffs here: https://lnkd.in/eRPmUkce --- As a special note. This is the first post I've done with a co-author: Tobasum Mandal , a Vanderbilt student who was a huge part of building the prototype and writing this. She was spectacular to work with. If you're hiring – hire her, especially if you need help with AI and especially if you're a startup. ...more ...more

We raised $4.8 million to make AI explain with video, not just text. Today, we are announcing Lamina Labs and Simi, our first product and the fastest way to make an explainer video. Give Simi a single prompt, document, or script, and it can generate a complete one-minute narrated explainer in as little as eight seconds, in more than 80 languages. It works like ChatGPT, except the answer is a video. This announcement means a lot to us for reasons that go beyond the funding. Kartikesh and I grew up in two of the most remote parts of Nepal. Neither of us grew up knowing what MIT, Y Combinator, or venture capital were. Years later, we met at MIT. Today, we are proud to be the first all-Nepalese founding team in Y Combinator history. The idea behind Lamina came from something both of us experienced growing up: difficult ideas are much harder when you do not have the right teacher, explanation, or visual in front of you. LLMs changed access to knowledge. Almost anyone can now ask a question and receive an answer instantly. But knowledge is not the same as understanding. The most intelligent models in the world still explain almost everything through paragraphs on a screen. Not because text is always the best way to teach, but because it has been the easiest medium for computers to generate. We believe that is changing. A student should be able to turn a difficult question into a visual lesson. A company should be able to turn documentation into a walkthrough. An AI agent should be able to show how it reached a conclusion, not just return another wall of text. That is why we built Simi. Simi is designed to create explanations that teach, not videos that merely look good. But Simi is only our first product. Lamina Labs is building fast, precise, and controllable video infrastructure for LLMs. Our goal is to let any model, agent, or application generate video at the moment an explanation is needed. The round was led by Foundation Capital , with participation from Link Ventures and Y Combinator . We are deeply grateful to everyone who believed in us, helped us get here, and gave two kids from Nepal the chance to build something much bigger than ourselves. This video tells our story. And we are only getting started.

We won 2nd Place at CrewAI hackathon in San Francisco At 12:51 AM on Sunday, my phone rang. I was home sick, completely unaware of the CrewAI Hackathon happening the next day, and ready to sleep off the weekend. Ali Amjad convinced me on the call to drop my plans and join him in CrewAI Hackathon. I said yes. Despite the fever, I showed up 30 minutes early at 8:30 AM so we could map out our vision. We didn't walk in with a pre built team. We built it on the fly. Around 10:00 AM, Kaushik Sivakumar casually walked in to say hello. Ali just looked at him and said, "You are in our team." Just like that, we had our technical foundation. Then about an hour and a half later, we realized our UI didn't feel right. We knew we needed to fix it. Somehow Arya Mishra showed up out of nowhere. Ali drafted her on the spot. She stepped in and completely transformed our user experience and presentation. While Ali had to leave before the presentation for a different event, Kaushik, Arya, and I got to work shaping the product story and the code. Together, we built ROOT 🥈 (2nd Place Winners!). Every time I joined a new company it took at least 1 week to get access to tools and technologies as it takes approval from different teams. We connected Zendesk with the CrewAI platform and built a custom full-stack architecture to house a swarm of 14 autonomous agents. Here is what Root does: Instantly reads the Zendesk ticket for a new hire (identifying their role, manager, and department). Autonomously determines the exact software, tech stack, and physical hardware that specific employee needs. Immediately dispatches tickets and emails to the IT and Security teams to provision those exact accesses. What used to take an entire week of manual bottlenecks now happens seamlessly in minutes. Here is the biggest takeaway from this wild weekend. We built an AI platform dedicated to perfect orchestration, but the real magic was the human orchestration. Hackathons are about finding the right people, trusting them fast, and creating the conditions where everyone can do their best work. Huge shout out to Ali for pushing us to our limits and Arya for making the UI and Khushak to work on the backend while I worked on the architecture of the product. I am extremely thankful to the CrewAI team for organizing this amazing hackathon. Happy to share that this past weekend, I worked with Praniil Nagaraj to win the ElevenLabs track at RocketHacks 2026, hosted by MLH and the University of Toledo. Lots of learnings from this one: 1. Don’t rush the beginning We dove straight into building without thinking enough about structure — file organization, data flow, and how components would connect. That led to avoidable friction later. A bit more upfront planning would have saved us a lot of time. 2. Less is sometimes more We tried to pack in too many features early on. There’s a hard limit to what you can realistically build in 24 hours. Things got much smoother once we focused on a few core problems and built around those. 3. Think beyond the product During judging, we were asked about the business model — and we didn’t have a great answer. It’s easy to focus purely on building, but viability matters too. Every project needs a story for how they sustain itself. 4. Integration is always harder than expected Individual pieces worked, but connecting everything together took longer than anticipated. Save some time to get things talking to each other. Definitely one of the most intense (and rewarding) builds I’ve done, can't wait for the next one.

I'm excited to share that I recently placed Top 5 at the inaugural University of Michigan - Stephen M. Ross School of Business x University of Michigan College of Engineering AI Hackathon with Ayush Madhav Kumar , Caleb Kosel , and Sajiv Jampani . We asked a simple question: Shouldn't exam feedback reflect concept mastery instead of just question accuracy? Our solution was an AI-powered, professor-side exam analyzer that turns question-level performance into concept-based competency scores. Given any question, our tool evaluates a student's understanding of: - The core concept being tested - The foundational concepts that may influence their understanding - Any downstream concepts that could be impacted by a gap in understanding It then compiles these insights into structured class/individual level reports that professors can use to gain insights into their class's understanding of the content and provide better, targeted feedback to students. As my first hackathon, this experience was especially impactful. Beyond my first time using the technical skills involved in the project, it challenged me to think critically about potential issues and possible solutions in the educational world. I'm grateful for the team and the experience. Time to carry this momentum forward.

activity.title: The more I see AI move into enterprise, the more I think the biggest constraint is not intelligence. It is execution. Most companies already know what they want to change. The challenge is making that change across Salesforce , NetSuite , SAP , Workday , ServiceNow , and the many dependencies connecting them, without adding more risk along the way. That work still requires a huge amount of specialized knowledge, manual coordination, and institutional memory. And too often, the people responsible for moving the business forward are also spending their time rediscovering why systems were configured a certain way five years ago. This is why Assemble caught my attention. Assemble is building an AI Solutions Engineer for enterprise IT. It maps dependencies across core systems, runs changes from a single interface, and verifies them against a shadow environment before they reach production. The important part is not simply that it can execute faster. It is that execution is designed to be controlled: blast-radius analysis before a change, auditable traces for every action, and a revertible ledger when something needs to be rolled back. I do not see this as replacing the people who understand these systems. I see it as giving those teams a better operating layer, one that helps them spend less time on repetitive implementation work and more time on architecture, judgment, and the projects that actually move the business forward. The organizations that make the most of AI may not be the ones experimenting with the most models. They may be the ones that become best at translating ambition into safe, repeatable execution. Where do you see the biggest constraint today, is it deciding what to change, or navigating the systems required to actually ship it? Feels like a 🥶 labor market! Yesterday the Fed held rates steady in a 9-3 vote. Three regional presidents wanted to hike. The majority wanted to hold. That's not consensus. That's a committee that genuinely doesn't agree on what the economy is doing. The June jobs report added 57,000 jobs, well below expectations. But unemployment ticked down. Wage growth moderated. What I do think is clear: this is a low-hire, low-fire market. Layoffs are not spiking. But hiring has slowed dramatically. Our data suggests that companies are cautious , and workers are staying put rather than taking risks on new roles. This kind of frozen market has its own risks in the long-term, including skills atrophy, which is especially concerning in the AI-age.

I’m excited to share that I’ve completed my summer internship at MaineHealth Institute for Research ! This has been one of my most memorable summers so far, and I’m incredibly honored to have had the opportunity to work under Dr. Matt Lynes on my project, “Multimodal Clustering of Post-Cardiac Arrest Syndrome (PCAS) Patients to Predict Clinical Outcome.” This summer was especially meaningful because it was my first opportunity to work with real-world human clinical data and use bioinformatics approaches. I developed a computational pipeline that integrated lipidomics data and immune cell profiles to identify distinct molecular subgroups of PCAS patients. I then used XGBoost to identify the molecular features that were most important in distinguishing these patient groups and predicting better responses to current standard treatments. Working with these two biological modalities showed me how integrating different layers of patient data can provide a more comprehensive picture of disease. More importantly, this experience gave me a new perspective on the potential of precision medicine: using patient-specific molecular information to better understand disease, predict outcomes, and potentially identify biological drivers that could inform more personalized approaches to care. Special thanks to Carolina Cora and Crystal V. for making my time in the lab so much happier, and to Dr. Andrea Tilden, Ph.D. for making all of this possible. And a huge thank you to Dr. Lynes for his mentorship and for giving me the opportunity to take on this project and grow as a researcher. I’m leaving this summer with so much gratitude, new skills, and excitement for what’s ahead! 🧬💻

When I first attended AI Camp during the summer of 2022, I could have never guessed how much my life trajectory would change... So, although a bit late, I want to thank everyone and share some of the invaluable knowledge I attained now that I have been involved at AI Camp for over a year! First off, thank you to the teams that constantly motivated me, gave me incredibly insightful information, and refined my skills while teaching me imperative new ones. Be detailed and specific, and be able to articulate all of the answers to yourself so you can do the same for others. 2. 👨‍🏫 Perfect your presentation skills. People who see the vision and go out of their way to pick up that new role not because they know it, but because they desire the company to succeed, are the individuals you need to achieve liftoff. We built a system that lets multiple people construct a city using only their brain signals! In just 48 hours Siddharth Manne , Emiliano Cuevas , and I built Inception - a multi-brain collaborative city generator - at the Global Neurohack Hackathon hosted at the frontiertower bringing teams around the world from Oxford University, UC Berkeley, Rice, Imperial, and more. No keyboards. No mice. No talking. Just brains. Multiple people wear OpenBCI EEG headsets simultaneously. Their combined neural signals detect emotional state in real time and that collective emotion continuously shapes the atmosphere, color, and feel of the world being built. We use neural symbiosis where not just one brain commands a machine, but multiple minds fuse together. Your brain sets the mood. Your eyes place the objects. Your voice summons the architecture. You speak a scene out loud, Black Forest Labs generates an image, that image is animated into a video, and Meta's TRIBE v2 - trained on 500+ hours of fMRI scans from 700+ people - predicts the exact neural activation pattern for what you're perceiving and decodes what gets built next. Through ElevenLabs, the city finds its voice, narrating the world as it dreams itself into existence. The bigger picture: everyone is stuck navigating 2D menus to express 3D ideas. We built a system where you don't describe what you want to build — you feel it, look at it, and speak it into existence. When design tools finally speak the language of human thought rather than forcing human thought to speak the language of design tools, the barriers between imagination and creation dissolve. That's the world we're building toward. Huge thanks to the organizers and shoutout to some awesome people we met during the hackathon: Matthew MacDougall , Luke Gordon , Morgan Hough, and more. publications.title: A Large Language Model-Powered Map of Metabolomics Research
publications.subtitle: bioRxiv
publications.description: We present a comprehensive map of the metabolomics research landscape, synthesizing insights from over 80,000 publications. Using PubMedBERT, we transformed abstracts into 768-dimensional embeddings that capture the nuanced thematic structure of the field. Dimensionality reduction with t-SNE revealed distinct clusters corresponding to key domains such as analytical chemistry, plant biology, pharmacology, and clinical diagnostics. In addition, a neural topic modeling pipeline refined with GPT-4o mini reclassified the corpus into 20 distinct topics-ranging from "Plant Stress Response Mechanisms" and "NMR Spectroscopy Innovations" to "COVID-19 Metabolomic and Immune Responses." Temporal analyses further highlight trends including the rise of deep learning methods post-2015 and a continued focus on biomarker discovery. Integration of metadata such as publication statistics and sample sizes provide additional context to these evolving research dynamics. An interactive web application (https://metascape.streamlit.app/) enables dynamic exploration of these insights. Overall, this study offers a robust framework for literature synthesis that empowers researchers, clinicians, and policymakers to identify emerging research trajectories and address critical challenges in metabolomics, while also sharing our perspectives on key trends shaping the field.

publications.title: IE-GADCI: An End-to-End Incoherence-Enhanced Generative Adversarial Deep Compressive Imaging
publications.subtitle: IEEE
publications.description: In this work, we present a new computational framework designed to jointly optimize both the illumination pattern and the image reconstruction algorithm for block-scanning SPI, under the principle of compressive sensing. Our architecture employs a neural network that learns the latent sparse representations of the scene and integrates information from both the image and sparsity domains to achieve high-resolution reconstructions with high computational efficiency. A key innovation of IE-GADCI is its optimization of the incoherence between the illumination pattern and the sparse representation, which substantially improves reconstruction fidelity. We validated the performance of IE-GADCI through numerical simulations on natural and biomedical image datasets.

Every silicon wave follows the same law. Most people see the term GPU and forget what the G actually stands for. Graphics. It was purpose-built for exactly that workload: rendering graphics, floating point math, managing lots of cores. It was never designed for AI. It was a battlefield promotion - better than a CPU, but not what anyone would build starting from a blank sheet of paper. If you zoom out, you’ll see the same pattern has repeated across 5 decades: - 70s-80s: Personal computers. Serial single-threaded, scalar performance, standard instruction set, perfectly suited to x86. - 90s: Graphics - a new workload with highly parallel floating-point operations, created a new chip. The GPU. - 00-10s: Mobile came along. It needed low power, a small form factor and always-on connectivity. Those constraints created the opportunity for ARM - a wildly successful business for two decades. Then around 2015, we saw it again through the lens of our portfolio at Foundation Capital : statistical inference over large datasets. AI workloads that are intensely data I/O bound and were ramping very, very steeply. Whenever you see a workload spiking that hard, there's an opportunity to replace the compute layer. So you ask the first-principles question: “If you were designing for this workload from scratch, what would you build?” You'd build what we built at Cerebras . New workloads deserve custom, purpose-built silicon. That's been the story of every silicon wave for 50 years. If you want to know where the next generational chip company comes from, don't watch the chips. Watch the workloads. Thanks again for a great conversation Oz Woloshyn

A year ago, Nick , Matthew , and I were building GroundControl during YC P25. Yesterday I went back to YC Startup School as a Friend of YC. In the last year, we've grown to serve hundreds of manufacturers around the world as a team of 14. A few insights that stuck out: 1. Your brain is still the fastest chip you own. Round-tripping to a model for things you already know how to reason through is often slower, not faster. 2. The lean startup playbook isn't the only playbook anymore. For years, "start narrow, find your wedge" was the only reliable path. Now there are real tailwinds for going bigger, faster. We've taken that approach as we now have 4 products across GroundControl. The question isn't lean vs. ambitious but which one actually matches the moment you're building in? 3. Acceleration is exponential. 6 years ago, the top LLM user was using ~100K tokens a month. Today, the top user uses 100M+. 4. Sam Altman's quote that stuck with me: He expects the next 6 months of model progress to feel as big as the last 2 years combined. Join us for the grand opening of our captivating exhibition showcasing the abandoned art works and redefining the concept of "abandonment." 🎆 😀 Exhibition Descriptions & Details: By the end of each art school’s semester, there are piles after piles of student artworks thrown out into the trash, taken into the dumpster to be buried, burned, destroted. The Catchers collected more than a hundred and seventy of these pieces from the previous fall and spring semesters, some stright from the bins, others right before the works were collectively disposed by the art schools in which they are created. Some pieces were never intentionally “abandoned”, and we hope to find their creators through this exhibition; others we obtained consent from the artists for them to be displayed and their stories to be told. But the *Tale of the Abandoned* wants to convey more than just about the stories of the salvaged works; we hope to shine light on the concept of “abandonment” itself, to invite our dear audience to join us in the contemplation of abandonement: How and why does it come about? When do we notice what we abandon, and when do we not? When we abandon something, where does it go? Can we ever truly abandon anything at all? … The list of questions go on, and we want you to add on to it. About The Catchers Curation: The Catchers' Curation is a non-profit curatorial team established and built for this very art exhibition project, consisting of 37 full-time students from universities across the globe. We noticed the large amount of abandoned art in the School of Visual Arts and the other schools we attend, which includes Pratt Institute, Fashion Institute of Technology, The New School and more. The Catchers run on the passion we have for art, the care we hold for artists, and the curiosity we choose to navigate the world with. When I joined Adobe , I thought I'd stay for 2 years. Ten years later, I'm still here. Not because that was the plan. In fact, I never really had a plan. Like many young professionals, I thought my career would be a series of stepping stones. Join. Learn. Move. Repeat. Simple. But careers have a funny way of ignoring our timelines. Over the last decade, I've seen people leave for bigger opportunities. I've seen people return. I've seen technologies rise and fall. I've seen "critical" issues disappear and "small" projects change careers. Most importantly, I've seen how differently a career looks from the inside compared to the outside. When we're young, we imagine successful careers as straight lines. Promotion. Promotion. Promotion. Reality looks more like a maze. There are detours. Plateaus. Unexpected opportunities. And sometimes, the biggest growth happens during the periods when it feels like nothing is happening. Looking back, one lesson stands out. Experience isn't just about the number of years. It's about the number of patterns you've seen. The difficult customer. The impossible deadline. The failed project. The unexpected success. Over time, you realize that many "new" problems are actually old problems wearing different clothes. That's what experience gives you. Not all the answers. Just better questions. When I joined Adobe , I thought success would come from constantly looking ahead. Ten years later, I've learned that sometimes growth comes from staying long enough to understand what everyone else is rushing past. And that's a lesson I didn't expect to learn.

publications.title: Shared Control of Assistive Robots through User-intent Prediction and Hyperdimensional Recall of Reactive Behavior (submitted)
publications.subtitle: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2023
publications.description: here is increasing interest in shared control for assistive robotics with adaptable levels of supervisedautonomy. In this work, we present a user-adaptive multi-layer shared control scheme for control of assistive devices. The system leverages the advantages of brain-inspired hyperdimensional computing (HDC) for classification & recall of reactive robotic behavior including high performance, computational efficiency and intelligent sensor fusion, to execute actuation based on the user’s goal while alleviating the burden of fine control. Using a multi-modal dataset of activities of daily living, we first recognize the user’s most recent behaviors, then predict the user’s next action based on their habitual action sequences, and finally, determine actuation through HDC recall-based shared control whichintelligently deliberates between the predicted action and sensor feedback-based autonomy. In this work, we independently implement each layer to achieve >92% accuracy and then integrate all the layers and discuss the combined performance and methods to reduce accumulated error.

publications.title: Brain-inspired multi-level control of an assistive prosthetic hand through emg task recognition
publications.subtitle: IEEE Biomedical Circuits and Systems Conference 2022 (Accepted)
publications.description: Brain-inspired hyperdimensional computing (HDC) has shown promise for highly accurate EMG-based gesture recognition owing to its few-shot learning capabilities, and robustness to noise and electrode placement variability. The simplistic paradigm is also ultra low-power and low latency, potentially enabling local and fast closed-loop control of assistive prosthetic devices. In this work, we propose a novel fully HDC multi-level sensor fusion prosthetic control scheme. While prior work has only utilized HDC for recognition of static gestures held for 5 seconds, prosthetic control depends on task recognition with continuously changing EMG signals. To achieve this, we collect a multi-sensor dataset for 6 activities of daily living with feedback sensors, detailed sub-tasks and two levels of timing complexity. Finally, we demonstrate task recognition accuracy of 91% on the continuously changing EMG data, contributing a basis on which higher levels of control can be designed.

publications.title: Examining the effects of variation of plasma conditions on the performance of high-energy long-pulse Brillouin amplifiers using one-and two-dimensional simulations
publications.subtitle: American Physical Society Division of Plasma Physics Meeting 2021
publications.description: The plasma Brillouin amplifier uses an ion acoustic wave (IAW) to transfer energy from a ''pump'' laser to a ''seed'' laser, and can generate short, high-intensity pulses without being subject to the damage limits of conventional optical systems. The concept is the subject of a feasibility study at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), and we have developed a two-dimensional time-dependent simulation code for studying Brillouin amplification in such high-energy long-pulse systems. We apply our code to the NIF parameters and test the robustness of the amplification process to the variation of plasma and laser conditions expected around the nominal experimental parameters, with particular attention paid to the non-trivial spatial variation of plasma density and temperature. We compare our 2D simulations with the results of a standard three-wave 1D model, showing that for non-zero crossing angle between pump and seed beams the 2D overlap geometry produces strong transverse variation resulting from asymmetric amplification not seen in 1D. We report detailed simulations that can be used to inform the planned experiments at NIF.

Today, we're excited to announce the winners of the inaugural Partcl × Hudson River Trading Macro Placement Challenge! Macro placement remains one of the most challenging optimization problems in modern physical design. Every macro placement decision influences wirelength, congestion, timing, and ultimately the quality of the finished chip. Despite decades of research, efficiently producing high-quality placements continues to be an open problem at the intersection of optimization, algorithms, machine learning, and high-performance computing. To encourage new ideas from the broader systems community, Partcl and Hudson River Trading launched this challenge with ~$30,000 in prizes. Participants were free to develop any placement strategy - from simulated annealing to reinforcement learning, graph neural networks, evolutionary algorithms, and hybrid approaches. The response exceeded our expectations. The competition received 223 registrations, with 132 verified eligible submissions. During evaluation we saw an impressive diversity of ideas, including force-directed optimization, convex optimization, GPU-accelerated placers, learned policies, analytical methods, and entirely novel placement heuristics. == Winners == 🥇 First Place: Archgen AI "Archgen" Archgen achieved the strongest overall performance among the finalists, consistently producing the best proxy cost across the benchmark suite. Their average proxy score for the ibm benchmarks was 0.9507 🥈 Runner-Up: Rishi Gottumukkala "Carrotato" Carrotato delivered an exceptionally competitive solution, finishing within a narrow margin of the winning submission while maintaining an efficient implementation with an average proxy cost of 0.9522 💡 Innovation Award: Arun Kumar "ArzunPD" While the Innovation Award is independent of leaderboard position, ArzunPD stood out for introducing one of the competition's most technically ambitious ideas: online machine learning inside the macro placement optimizer itself. Final rankings were determined using the challenge's proxy cost metric. We believe this is an important result. Proxy metrics have become the standard objective in much of macro placement research because they are fast to compute and make large-scale experimentation practical. However, our results suggest that optimizing proxy objectives alone is not sufficient to produce production-ready macro placements. We would like to thank everyone who participated. Building a competitive macro placer requires substantial engineering effort, and every submission contributed valuable ideas to the open physical design community. Thank you to our guest judge Patrick McEwen for his hard work and commitment to a fair judging process. We're especially grateful to Hudson River Trading for sponsoring this competition and supporting open research in EDA and high-performance computing. Thank You! ...more ...more

I'm excited to share our first SOTA model! FeyNoBg removes the background from your images. Try it out here: https://lnkd.in/eJdKMJP2 Background removal is one of the most common yet under-appreciated use cases of AI. It is also extremely complicated. Models can easily be thrown off by soft edges, blur, and fine objects. FeyNoBg is able to handle all of those cases. We took a novel interpretability first approach to training this model. We first understood the architecture of BiRefNet, an existing model, focusing on how each of its layer contributes to the final product. We discovered that the third stage of its feature extractor does quite a lot of work! The model depends on the information here for both detecting the subject and finding its boundary! 👇 We built a portfolio robo-advisor that tracks the market, winning 1st place at Waterloo's annual CFM Case Competition! While beating the market often gets the spotlight, doing so consistently is difficult, even for professionals. In practice, many investors are better served by portfolios that prioritize stability, safety, and controlled exposure rather than chasing high returns. So, along with Jaimin Patel and Frank Lin , we built a market-tracking portfolio robo-advisor. As students, our goal wasn't to outsmart the market, but to understand how to meet it. We focused on minimizing unnecessary deviation, managing risk, and building a system that behaves predictably under real market conditions. 🛠️ What we built: - A Python-based investment engine selecting 10–25 stocks - Dynamic weight adjustments using rolling beta, volatility, covariance, and correlation - A scorecard framework benchmarking each stock directly against a blended TSX / S&P 500 index - Defensive sector tilting (e.g., Healthcare, Utilities) to stabilize performance during market noise 📈 The result? After running live for 5 trading days with continuously updated market data, our portfolio achieved a 3.23% return, finishing only 0.70% off the blended TSX/S&P 500 benchmark despite a short window and earning 1st place. What mattered most to me wasn’t just the win, but the process: - Designing signals that update daily, not in hindsight - Thinking in terms of risk, stability, and relative movement not just returns - Seeing how small modelling decisions compound when exposed to real markets I am grateful for my teammates and for a program that gives us room to experiment, compete, and learn by doing. Introducing the Mercor AI Consumer Index (ACE), our benchmark for measuring how frontier models handle the everyday tasks people use AI for across Shopping, Food, Gaming, and DIY. The results show a clear gap between expectations and performance: even the top model scores only 56.1% overall, and models fail grounding checks between 29% and 62% of the time, often hallucinating basic details like prices or links. ACE introduces a methodology built for real-world reliability, with hurdle criteria that require solving the user’s core objective and grounding criteria that penalize hallucinations. We also have criteria labels that reveal where models break down: strong performance on simple quantity checks, but much weaker on nuanced judgments like Gaming compatibility and DIY safety guidance. We’re open-sourcing 80 cases on Hugging Face and our full evaluation harness on GitHub to support transparency and reproducibility. Together with APEX, our benchmarks now measure both economic value and consumer value, because AI’s usefulness depends on how well it performs even beyond the workplace. 2025 changed my life in 100 ways Not exaggerating. Here’s why I have been MIA: 2025 started with a very chill version of me — figuring out life after high school while studying for my ISC 12th board exams. In January, I attended my high school farewell and applied to the top 5 unis in the world for a CS undergrad. I was completely set on taking a gap year, and building The Founderly in Bangalore. My mom convinced me to just “shoot my shot.” In February, I got into UC Berkeley MET. My life changed overnight. March was boards season. And for the first time in my life, marks didn’t feel like the center of my universe. From April to July, I maximised time with family and friends. Tiny trips. Long conversations. Silent realisations that everything was about to change. Then July took me to France to represent India at the ETEAM International Math Olympiad. In the first round, our team was second last. By the end, we finished second overall. (Thanks Lodha Group and Jane Street for this opportunity) That comeback still feels surreal. It was the first time I experienced how quickly things can turn when you refuse to give up. And then came August and September. The hardest months of my life. New university. New country. New systems. New everything. I was converting dollars to rupees in restaurants. Miles to kms in my head. Relearning how to communicate. Getting used to being misunderstood, and misunderstanding others. Back home, I was consistently at the top 10% of my grade. At Berkeley, I was surrounded by people just as driven, just as talented — if not more. I didn’t end with the GPA I was used to. Not even close. But I ended with perspective. I met some of the smartest and most inspiring people I know. My world became infinitely bigger, yet strangely smaller at the same time. Berkeley broke my confidence in a 1000 ways. But it also expanded my ambition in ways I didn’t even know were possible. Before coming here, I didn’t even know the kinds of things I could achieve. I didn’t know they were in the realm of possibility for someone like me. 2025 didn’t just change where I live. It changed how I see myself. And I’m just getting started. PS - I guess we are back on the Linkedin grind 🙌

Reforged Labs is winding down. We spent three years building AI creative tools for mobile game studios spending $500M+/yr on ads But it wasn't going to become the company we raised to build. The market is small. Our best customers signed six-figure contracts... but there aren't many studios at that scale. We tried expanding beyond gaming. It didn't work well enough. Then AI changed dramatically over the last few months. The models became so capable that we rewrote major parts of our own product around them. And I think our customers, some of the most sophisticated teams in gaming, will soon be able to build much of this themselves The gap we were selling into is closing. We could have kept Reforged going as a smaller business. The revenue was real. But I'd rather end it clearly than shrink it slowly. What I'll remember isn't the ending. It's a team split across the Vietnam & and the US ... shipping into some of the biggest studios in the world + a fraction of the people those studios have To that team: best people I've ever worked with. A few are still looking. This weekend, my team ( Aryan Jain , Ryan Ding ) and I built Train of Thought, a tool to run two LLM agents in parallel and implement a type of chain of thought thinking! By using two agents to break down a prompt, generate a chain of thoughts, and verifying subproblem outputs, we saw accuracy and safety improvements over a one-shot approach. This was inspired by OpenAI 's recent o1 model as well as research in the field of multi-agent LLMs. Currently, the project uses two instances of Google 's Gemini Flash 1.5 model, but this approach can be generalized to any number and type of models. Potential Applications: - Safety: Ensure agents are obeying safety policies by using each agent to moderate the other. - Accuracy: Improve accuracy of the overall system by breaking down prompts and ensuring each subproblem is solved correctly. - Backtracking: Agents backtrack if incorrect output is seen at any stage. - Multi-Agent Learning: One agent can learn from another agent by using it to provide overall reasoning about a prompt. In the future, this system can use a collection of models, each with their own specialties. Overall, working on this project was a blast and a great learning opportunity for all of us. I have always held strong conviction in Kodiak ’s leadership position. It is, of course, nice to see it confirmed in independent metrics like The Road to Autonomy® 's Autonomous Truck Index. Kodiak’s technology is deployed in 35 driverless trucks, as of June 30, the largest customer owned-and-operated fleet of semis in the world.

July was my last month at Kodiak . The past 8 years have been exciting and incredibly rewarding. I started about 5 weeks after the company was founded with nothing but a laptop and a rack full of snacks, and led the company as CTO to the first full commercial launch of a driverless trucking fleet - 24/7 operations, owned and operated by the customer - in 2024, followed by Kodiak’s public listing on NASDAQ in 2025. As of June 2026, Kodiak had 35 driverless trucks deployed at the customer’s site, having operated 40,000+ cumulative paid hours without anyone in the cabin. The latest software release further increased efficiency by 30%, all in a harsh environment with oncoming, third-party traffic. And it also isn’t just the one vehicle, because not all customers want the same: we built several driverless platforms, from big semis to offroad vehicles, that could operate safely in their respective environments. Most recently, the team delivered the first driverless daycab that I know of, on yet another new OEM base platform and with a new Gen7 generation of autonomy hardware. This isn’t just technology, it’s a full product that is actually useful to customers - and that product focus has been in Kodiak’s DNA from day one. Behind the scenes, the reality of Physical AI is amazingly complex: It took designing a system from the ground up that could meet the rigor of a full safety assessment to launch in 2024 and repeatedly after; finding and hiring hundreds of excellent people to refine and execute the plan; coordinating OEMs, suppliers, contract manufacturers, and partners around the world and earning their trust over years; real-world testing in both hot and icy conditions from the Permian to Michigan, and many interstates between; testing in simulated environments that reflect all of those conditions with well understood fidelity; and aligning the software, hardware, and systems engineering so we could operate safely and efficiently at the same time. I was part of it at every step, leading, helping, and motivating; but the real credit goes to the team at Kodiak who did the hard work on the ground and made it happen. I keep being impressed by what this team is able to do, often on tight timelines and tighter budgets. I’ve seen first hand how listening well, sharing insights, and helping others grow will exponentially increase the impact of an organization. Thank you for giving me the opportunity and trust to lead you through the ups and downs every startup goes through on the way to success. It’s been an incredible experience! Now it’s time to make space for the next generation of leaders at Kodiak. I've been enjoying time with family, both here in the US and in Austria, and reconnecting with people I haven't had a chance to talk to for way too long. If you're around, let's chat - I'd love to catch up.

projects.description: Boing is a Mindustry server wrapper that adds a Discord bot interface, making it easy to control and manage private game servers. Boing streamlines multiplayer gaming and enhances community play between friends. It supports the slash commands enabled by Discord API v3 and features remote usage, so players can run and interact with their server without needing direct access to the host machine. It was built mainly in Node.js, using the Axios and Discord.js libraries.

You can move your chats between Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor now. Here’s how. Recently, I wanted to resume working on a project I had started a few months ago in Cursor. Having gotten more accustomed to Claude Code, I wanted to use Claude Code instead of Cursor moving forward. However, my Cursor chats held context that I couldn’t port into Claude, making for a rough handoff. The great thing about writing software in 2026 is there's no reason to wait for solutions to your problems. I vibe coded an MVP by lunchtime on a random Sunday when I felt like it. My initial challenge of porting Cursor chats to Claude Code was solved. But then I got ambitious: I wanted to implement the opposite migration path, as well as add support for other coding agents. This required some creativity - telling Claude to “add Codex support, make no mistakes” would be futile, because it had no way to verify its work without me manually attempting migrations and visually confirming everything looked correct over and over. So then I built my own end-to-end verification loop for CLI development. The end result was that Claude could add support for other agents without any intervention on my part! This became a distinct project that deserves a separate writeup. In the meantime, try out agent-migrator. You can install it with one command: uv tool install agent-migrator Then, in any project directory where you’ve used Claude Code CLI, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, or Cursor IDE, simply run: agent-migrator Pick your source and target agents, select the chats you want to migrate, and submit. The chats you started with one coding agent instantly become visible to another - a useful ability considering Claude’s rather disappointing uptime, and the fact that a different company releases the latest “most powerful” coding model every two weeks. It’s open source. Check out the repo at the link in the comments! I even included a Claude Code plugin that auto-migrates your chat when you start hitting API errors. ...more

Won another YC Hackathon, and this time I met Garry Tan ! Last Saturday I was at my fourth Y Combinator hackathon, where we were tasked with using Garry Tan's "AI brain" framework, GBrain. GBrain ingests knowledge in any format, recalling information coherently over long periods of time and large volumes of data. It's meant to act as an extension of yourself or the sum of all your organization's knowledge. For this project, my teammate Holly T. leaned into her research experience in the medical field, ultimately identifying the problem we aimed to solve: junior radiologists need a way to improve their ability to analyze scans even when senior colleagues aren't available to assess their work. We didn't just guess that this problem existed. We first spoke to Yuva Krishnapillai , a Stanford-based brain researcher and founder whose insights offered initial validation for our idea. During the event, we even managed to chat with Dr. Michał Nedoszytko MD, PhD , the cardiologist who famously won at Anthropic 's global hackathon. After we demoed what we had built by that point, we asked upfront if he would find the product useful if we completed it and he were our target user, and he said yes! Filled with confidence, we doubled down on implementing a few points of feedback he had offered, and soon enough we submitted our project. We demoed live on stage, and then eagerly waited for the judges to deliberate. As someone who's been to several YC hackathons, this one held more weight than usual since Garry himself was among the judges. Eventually, it was time for the winners to be announced. Team after team walked onstage and posed for photos - and then they called up our team, Cortex! We thought we misheard the announcer for a moment, and then rushed to the stage. Turns out we were a winner in the GBrain track! This time around I didn't win cash... but I did get to exchange contact info with Garry! And he gave us signed hats. In any case, this hackathon was the first time I explored GStack and GBrain, as well as the first time I built anything for the healthcare industry. The whole experience was very inspiring, and I'm looking forward to the next hackathon. Thanks once again to my teammate Holly and to the event organizers! P.S. I've started going to hackathons every single weekend while I'm in SF. It's not about stacking up wins. Every hackathon is an opportunity to broaden your horizons, both in terms of technical experience and meeting new people. Most hackathons will encourage participants to build projects that relate to a given niche, or that utilize specific technologies. Those events are great for pushing yourself out of your comfort zone; before coming to SF, I had never built projects involving voice agents, edge inference, ChatGPT addons, Meta glasses, prediction markets, generative video, and the list goes on. Nothing was stopping me from exploring those technologies on my own, but hackathons forced me to actually become competent in them within a short time frame. Moreover, hackathons are an excellent source of inspiration as a prospective entrepreneur. I've found that attending these events keeps me ahead of the curve in terms of emerging technologies and the types of problems they can solve. Generally, I think there's a lot of overlap between good hackathon ideas and good startup ideas - the winning projects usually have identified a genuine pain point felt by real people which they've solved using innovative technology. Having to build useful, demoable products within a single day (or even just a few hours!) each weekend helps me train that entrepreneurial muscle as I explore my own ideas and come across new problems to solve. On the non-technical side, hackathons are also an excellent way to meet interesting people and push yourself out of your comfort zone. Outside of college-affiliated hackathons, I often find that I'm among the youngest in the room, but that's not a bad thing! At those events, I'm often surrounded by startup founders, senior engineers, top researchers, and serious builders who I can always learn something from. Simultaneously, I sometimes still run into people younger than myself - even high school students - who inspire me through their boldness and creativity. In the same vein, hackathons are an easy way to get noticed. Some of my best-performing posts on LinkedIn have been about hackathons I've gone to, and the projects I've built have made me much more noticeable. Of course, the people you make an impression on when you demo at these events can be highly valuable, too - consider TreeHacks , HackMIT , or the various Y Combinator hackathons I've gone to recently, for example! Anyways, I'm heading to yet another hackathon today over at UC Berkeley, and some bigger ones later this month. If you'd like to team up at a hackathon in the bay sometime, send me a message! And if a detailed breakdown about my hackathon strategies would be useful, do let me know. publications.description: With developments in miniature UAVs, the problem of flocking has gained significant interest in both academia and industry, with applications in ISR, EW, and communication missions. This paper presents a flocking control scheme for a fleet of fixed-wing UAVs with constrained non-holonomic kinematics. The scheme is based on the flocking algorithms of Olfati-Saber and modified dynamic feedback linearization and demonstrates significant improvements in maneuverability and reliability, which are vital for mission performance. The improvements in efficacy and reliability of the scheme are proved through simulations and a Monte Carlo study. With the proposed scheme, a flock of fixed-wing UAVs can reliably form and traverse any time-parameterized trajectory.

Finally secured the YC sticker! This past weekend, Josh Rodriguez , Jack Cappo , Ming Jin Yong , John Peng , & I competed at Y Combinator ’s RoboHacks and built ID0, the agentic hardware robot. Robots today are limited by one thing: their hands. We keep trying to build a single “perfect” gripper, and it ends up being mediocre at most tasks. So we asked: What if the robot just built the right tool for the job? ID0 scans its environment, understands its task, and generates a modular custom end effector using programmatic CAD. It 3D prints it, picks it up, and switches between tools autonomously. But this goes beyond this demo. If robots can make simple tools, it can evolve to more complex tools with sensors, motors, and magnets. AI can simulate thousands of design options and converge on the optimal design before printing anything. We envision this as the future of robotics, from robots learning software skills to custom building the hardware agents/tools necessary to complete any task. Built in 36 hours. publications.description: Abstract: The therapeutic cloning of humans is a philosophically interesting issue at this particular point in time, as biological research has found new uses to address increasingly prominent global healthcare challenges while minimizing the risks that ethicists of the twentieth century had once deemed great enough to dismiss all genetic engineering as wrong. Simultaneously, the gap between patients who require organs and those who receive transplants is widening. Patients awaiting organ transplantation who have not yet died and those who experience organ rejection post-transplantation suffer greatly diminished quality of life, the cost of millions of dollars to support their treatment, and a future of uncertainty. Genetically cloning human embryos, whose stem cells can be harvested and stimulated to develop into the desired one-to-one organ, is a lucrative solution to this trifold crisis of cost, suffering, and death. Underlying this promising solution are questions of ‘when morally valuable life begins’ and ‘at what point it may still be ethical to terminate an embryo’. I will first defend the moral significance of what I call passive embryonic potential... (Professor Blecher)

Security is the last part of the stack still built on the assumption that a human is watching. Everything else an engineering team touches has already been rebuilt for machine speed. The data warehouse. The deploy pipeline. The code editor itself. Each one got replaced the moment the old, human-paced version turned into the bottleneck. The security operations center is the holdout. It still sits a person in front of a queue & asks them to keep pace with software. Today Cursor goes public as an Artemis Security customer, & it's the clearest sign yet that the holdout is falling. A company operating at Cursor's velocity was never going to route detection & response through a console designed for a slower decade. Artemis now processes 10b+ events daily & resolves 96% of investigations autonomously. The human is left with the fraction that needs judgment, not the fraction a staffing plan happened to allow. This is a category flip, not a one-off vendor swap. The AI-native SOC will do to legacy security tooling what the cloud warehouse did to the on-prem database. Cursor is early. The rest of the market is running the same math right now. We're proud to back Shachar , Dan , & the Artemis team.

activity.title: 🎉 Wrapping up Day 3: Engineering, and with it, the final night of VISA: The Insider Case, I keep coming back to one feeling: gratitude. Over the past three days, this series became more than just a set of career panels. It became a space where students could hear honest stories about what it really takes to grow into competitive fields — not just the highlights, but also the uncertainty, the setbacks, and the discipline behind the progress. ⚙️ For Engineering Day, we were incredibly grateful to be joined by Hung Pham , Linh Ha , and Vien Nguyen , who each brought a different but equally valuable perspective. Hung Pham helped students think more intentionally about the CS journey early on: exploring different paths, building experience before chasing prestige, and taking freshman and sophomore years seriously as a time to experiment, apply, and grow. Linh Ha shared a perspective that felt especially real and grounding — that the path is not linear, going from 0 to 1 is often the hardest part, and consistency, mentorship, and trusting your own timeline matter more than comparison. Vien Nguyen challenged students to think more deeply about what makes a project meaningful: not just building something that works, but understanding the problem, designing thoughtfully, communicating clearly, and turning projects into real stories of engineering growth. To everyone who attended across all three days, thank you for showing up with curiosity, openness, and energy. Your questions, conversations, and willingness to learn are what made this series feel alive. 🙌 And to the Vietnamese International Student Association at USF e-board, thank you all for the care and work behind the scenes that made all of this possible. If there is one thing this 3-day series reminded me, it is this: no path is perfectly clear at the beginning, but hearing honest stories from people a few steps ahead can make the journey feel a lot more possible. 💙 ✨ Thank you to every speaker, attendee, and team member who helped make VISA: The Insider Case so meaningful. This was a special one.

I just concluded my summer at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory , where I researched how satellite megaconstellations could use onboard vision-language models to detect & triage natural disasters, and coordinate follow-up observations across multiple satellites, with no ground-in-the-loop. As part of the FAME AI group, I combined edge-deployable VLMs such as Gemma with graph-based orchestration, allowing models on different satellites to pass context and coordinate decisions as a multi-agent system. I began by benchmarking existing VLMs and fine-tuning them for disaster-detection tasks. I then built an orchestration harness that carried observations from detection through triage and follow-up planning. I tested the system using a time-series simulation of the core coordination loop across satellites under the hardware constraints of space systems. One highlight was meeting with Liquid AI and other commercial partners to discuss edge intelligence. Those conversations pushed me to communicate the system’s capabilities and limitations clearly and gave me a broader view of how the research connects across academic and commercial settings. I also enjoyed working alongside other interns exploring complementary approaches to natural-disaster detection, which showed me how many technical disciplines contribute to the same operational problem. I’m especially grateful to my mentors Steve, Jake, and Josh. They provided me excellent advice and direction, but also gave me room to experiment, make decisions, and work through difficult problems independently. This research remains deeply interesting to me, and I’ll continue working on it alongside several independent and team projects that I hope to share soon.

What happens when a natural disaster destroys the infrastructure you need to call for help? California constantly faces the threat of earthquakes and wildfires. In 1906, the San Francisco earthquake ruptured nearly 300 miles of the San Andreas Fault. If a disaster of that scale struck today, buildings could collapse, power could disappear, and cellular and Wi-Fi networks could go dark. If you were trapped beneath rubble and your phone displayed “No Service,” how would you reach first responders? That question led to SafeRelay. Which I'm happy to share helped me and my teammates: Zhiyu Wen and Rishabh B. win 1st place in the Social Impact track at JacHacks SF last Sunday! SafeRelay turns ordinary smartphones into a peer-to-peer emergency communication network. A survivor creates a distress packet containing their location, condition, and request for help. The packet then travels between nearby phones over Bluetooth Low Energy. Each device stores the message and relays it forward without requiring cellular service or Wi-Fi. Even if none of the nearby phones are connected to the internet, the packet continues hopping from device to device. The first phone that eventually reaches any form of internet connectivity uploads the message chain to our server. From there, our Jac-powered operations console allows first responders to: • View off-grid emergency reports on a map • Understand a survivor’s location and situation • Prioritize incidents based on urgency • Compare incoming reports with live USGS and NWS hazard data We also integrated on-device AI using Apple’s Foundation Models framework. During an emergency, fear and stress can make it difficult to think clearly. Because the model runs directly on the phone, a survivor can describe their situation and receive survival tips even when the cloud is completely unreachable. It is not a replacement for professional emergency guidance, but it brings useful intelligence to the exact moment when connectivity and clear thinking may both be unavailable. We used Capacitor for the mobile shell and CoreBluetooth for the native iOS radio bridge, the part that could only be properly tested using physical phones. Thank you to Jason Mars , Vatsal Shah , Lingjia Tang , the entire JacHacks team, and Jaseci Labs for creating such an incredible event and technology. Also, thank you to Founders, Inc. for a wonderful place to hack and build our idea. One thing I am learning while trying to get Deadlink into real pilots: a yes is not the same thing as a path to yes. Someone can like the idea. They can say the problem is real. They can even want the demo. But if the next step needs 5 people, 3 approvals, a procurement process, and a budget cycle, that is not the same as "we can try this next week." I used to think pricing was mostly: "what is this worth?" Now I think early pricing is also: "what can this person actually approve without turning it into a whole process?" That sounds boring. It is not. For a startup, the difference between useful and buyable is massive. Especially in public safety / drones, where people are busy, budgets are weird, and nobody wants to add another tool unless it clearly solves a painful thing. So I am trying to get better at asking the real question earlier. Not just: "do you want this?" But: "what would make this easy to actually try?" Very unglamorous lesson. Probably one of the most useful ones so far. For people who have sold pilots into gov, public safety, healthcare, logistics, or any ops-heavy market: what made your first pilot actually buyable?

projects.title: Fit-Plant
projects.description: Fit-Plant is an advanced digital soil meter developed as part of the Innovation Challenge at the Center for Entrepreneurship. The device integrates NPK (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium), light (BH1750), and soil moisture sensors with an ESP32 microcontroller to deliver real-time plant health insights. Using Arduino, we programmed the sensors to collect data and transmit it to a Next.js web app built with Python Flask, React JS, and Tailwind CSS. The web app compares sensor readings to optimal benchmarks from a dataset tailored to specific plants, providing actionable care recommendations to users. On the business side, I conducted due diligence on the agTech industry, performed competitor analysis, developed a revenue model, and identified key differentiators for market positioning. I also created and presented a pitch deck to local entrepreneurs in Cincinnati, showcasing Fit-Plant's potential for innovation and scalability in the agTech sector.

projects.description: At Hack Harvard 2024, my team and I developed Just Hurry!, a disaster relief platform that uses machine learning models built with scikit-learn and TensorFlow to predict hurricane impact zones in real time. The platform efficiently allocates resources such as food, water, and medical supplies by analyzing key factors like wind speed, air pressure, and population density. Built in under 36 hours, Just Hurry! enables relief organizations to register resources and allows users to request help or volunteer. We utilized ReactJS, Next.js, Python Flask, MongoDB, and Palantir Foundry for seamless data visualization and aid distribution.

What happens when you put 500 autonomous agents in a world with limited food, money, energy and health — and let them figure out how to survive? Over the past few weeks, I’ve been building Agent World, a multi-agent simulation to learn reinforcement learning from the ground up. Each agent lives for up to 1,200 simulated days and has four possible actions: work, rest, buy food, or form an alliance. Every decision has a tradeoff. Working earns money, but consumes food and energy. Buying food helps survival, but costs money. Resting restores the agent, but sacrifices an opportunity to earn. Agents can also trade with others, remember previous interactions, and form alliances. I initially built the learning system using tabular Q-learning. But as the state space became more complex, I wanted the agents to generalize rather than simply memorize state-action combinations. So I replaced the Q-table with a neural network and gradually built out a Deep Q-Network (DQN) — implementing each component individually so I could understand why it was necessary: → Neural Q-function approximation → ε-greedy exploration → Experience replay → Mini-batch training → Bellman targets → Terminal-state handling → A separate target network with periodic synchronization One of my favorite realizations while building this was that the agents themselves effectively create the training dataset by living. 500 agents × 1,200 days can generate up to 600,000 experiences in a single episode. Those experiences enter a replay buffer, random batches are sampled, and the shared neural network continuously updates its weights based on what worked — and what very much did not. The interesting part now is no longer getting the DQN to run. It’s figuring out what it actually learns. Does survival improve across episodes? Does it learn when sacrificing wealth for food is worthwhile? Does cooperation become strategically useful? What happens to wealth inequality? And perhaps most importantly: does the behavior I want actually match the reward function I designed? That last question has already been one of the biggest lessons from this project: An RL agent doesn't optimize what you intended. It optimizes what you rewarded. Now moving into longer training runs, reward-function tuning, and evaluating the trained policy against baseline strategies. Should you chase hype or ignore it? The tech industry has been debating this for decades. So Sequoia Capital , we dug into 20 years of hype data. This summer, I worked with Sequoia intern Oliver Cho to measure hype over the past 2 decades. The chart below ranks the most hyped topics on Hacker News for every year since 2007. Under each year sits the most valuable company founded that year. Here are a few observations: 1/ The top company founded in a given year is rarely related to the hype of that period. Airbnb was founded in 2008, when the top topic was Google. Uber arrived in 2009, while the conversation revolved around low-level programming. Anthropic came in 2021, while the internet was consumed by crypto. Chasing hype rarely leads to enduring outcomes. The top companies of recent years have yet to be decided. 2/ New trends announce themselves five to six years early. LLMs first cracked the top 15 in 2016 and took until 2022 to hit #1. AI coding entered at #12 in 2021 and tops the list in 2026. Crypto entered in 2011 before 2017 and 2021 peaks. “New” trends don’t appear out of nowhere, and internet subcommunities are often the first to know where the puck is headed. 3/ Long-term “hype” is a durable signal. The “Musk-Verse” has been a top 15 topic for every one of the past 14 years. Sustained attention on the internet is rare and tends to mark something real. Next up, we want to run the same analysis with sources like X and LinkedIn. If that's of interest, give us some encouragement and we'll share the results.
